title: New year: begin now
hookLine: a new year, and Seneca would say begin now, not tomorrow (Letters 1)

lines: A FRESH NOTEBOOK IN LATE DECEMBER.
cards: Late December, a kitchen table, a fresh notebook. Starting January first: run three times a week, call Grandma every Sunday, finally read the big book on the shelf. Writing it is the easy part.
It also quietly buys a week off. Today begins a short stretch of the path called the turning year: the calendar's markers, seen from the porch. It may not be January where you are, and that's fine.
Seneca's first letter to his friend Lucilius has an opinion about every fresh notebook, whatever the date.

teach.b: First, how the letter opens. Seneca tells Lucilius to claim himself for himself. In Latin it's three short words: vindica te tibi.
Set yourself free, take yourself back. From what? From the way time leaks out of a life.
Some time is snatched from us, some is quietly stolen, and some simply slips away.
The worst loss, he says, is the time wasted through carelessness, and most of a life goes by while we're doing something else, or nothing at all, or the wrong thing. Third, the turn for a new year.

teach.h: WHILE WE DELAY, LIFE RUNS PAST.
teach.b: While we put things off, he writes, life runs past. So hold on to every hour. Take hold of today's task, and you'll depend less on tomorrow.
He doesn't say make a list for next month. He says now. Fourth, his honesty.
Seneca admits he hasn't mastered this. He keeps an account of his time, like a careful but not very successful spender: he can tell you what he's lost and why. Not a grand plan for a new self.
A new year can begin on any Tuesday; the calendar just gives you an excuse. And a look back at the week: the wheel turns. Whose house is this word living in right now.
Constancy. Understand it. Examine the thought.
Virtue, not toughness. Begin now. A week of people after the ancients, carrying the porch into new centuries.

how: Readers of Seneca often treat any day as a fresh start, taking one small step toward a plan today instead of waiting for a new week, month or year.

o: a fresh start that only counts if it's January first
a time to plan a whole new self for next year
the calendar's turning point, a reminder to begin today

s: Seneca says he has fully mastered not wasting time
he admits he keeps an account like a careful but not very successful spender.
Seneca's first letter tells Lucilius to hold on to every hour
take hold of today's task, and you'll depend less on tomorrow.
Seneca told Lucilius to plan big changes for later
his advice is to begin now, not tomorrow.

games.q: it's late December and you have a plan for a better life. what would Seneca say?
o: wait for January first, for a clean start
begin one small part of it today
games.why: while we delay, he says, life runs past; hold on to today's hour.

practice: Think of one thing you've been saving for a better start, a fresh week, a new month, January, and shrink it until it fits inside today: not run three times a week, but walk to the corner; not the big book, but its first page.
Picture yourself doing it, and rest in knowing the beginning is already close.

wordCard.voice: New year: a turning point on the calendar, and for Seneca a reminder that the only day you can begin is this one. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca's Letters 1.1: claim yourself for yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: begin now. One hour, held, is already a start. That's a week, and day six hundred sixty-five.
